books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text: Postcard view of Hull House, Chicago, early 1900s. The red-brick Hull House complex fills a city street corner: a tall main building with gabled roofs and rows of windows, joined to lower wings stretching down the block, with young trees and a lamppost along the sidewalk and the words “THE HULL HOUSE, CHICAGO” printed in red at the upper right.
stimulus.source_note: Vintage V.O. Hammon (Chicago) postcard of Hull House, early 1900s. Image file: Wikimedia Commons, The Hull House, Chicago (front). Public domain.

stem: The size and solidity of the Hull House complex in the photograph best support which conclusion?

figures.alt: Color postcard of the red-brick Hull House settlement complex at a Chicago street corner, with the words THE HULL HOUSE, CHICAGO printed at upper right.
figures.caption: Hull House, Chicago, early 1900s postcard

options.text: Settlement houses were large, permanent buildings in city neighborhoods
Settlement houses were small, temporary shelters for newcomers
options.misconception: Reads a large brick complex as small and temporary.

options.text: Settlement houses were built by the federal government
options.misconception: Credits the federal government with a privately founded house.

options.text: Settlement houses served only native-born Americans living nearby
options.misconception: Limits a settlement house to native-born Americans.

rationales.A: The photograph shows a tall brick main building with lower wings stretching down the block — a large, solid complex, not a small or temporary shelter.
rationales.B: The photograph shows a large brick complex, not a small or temporary shelter.
rationales.C: The photograph does not show who built Hull House. Background: settlement houses were founded by private reformers, not by the federal government.
rationales.D: The photograph does not show whom Hull House served. Background: Hull House served its immigrant neighbors, not only native-born Americans.
rationales.general:
Look at what the photograph shows.
1. The postcard shows a tall brick main building with gabled roofs and rows of windows.
2. Lower wings stretch down the block, with young trees and a lamppost along the sidewalk.
3. A building that big, in brick, is large and permanent, not small or temporary.
4. The photograph shows size and solidity, not who built it or whom it served.
Remember: a photograph proves what it shows, not what it leaves out.
